Although histopathology examinations represent a vital diagnostic tool for diseases, primarily cancer, advancements in the last few decades have enabled the significant automation of area tasks such as region of interest selection and target object detection, including nuclei. Consequently, this study introduces a novel nucleus detection system built on the features of HematoPath Automatic Detection (HPAD). This approach adopts a sequential design known as W-Net, which refines the primary content features extracted by a stripped-down version of V-net using the loss functions weighted by spatial location. To assess performance, comprehensive evaluations were conducted on the HKPU Automatic Detection (HPAD) dataset, comprising 1,024 images gathered from five distinct institutions. When pitted against established methods like HistoPathology Nucleus Detector (HPND), Markov Random Field (MRF), and deep learning models U-Net and R-Vnet using both mean and spatially-aware metrics, the results demonstrate the system's superior accuracy and robustness, underscoring the distinct advantages provided by spatially optimized loss functions within a sequential architecture for nucleus detection.

Consider a non-archimedean local field $F$ with characteristic not equal to 2, and let $G$ be either a special odd-orthogonal group, $\text{SO}_{2r+1}(F)$, or a symplectic group, $\text{Sp}_{2r}(F)$. This work proves the local converse theorem for these classical groups $G$: specifically, given two irreducible admissible generic representations sharing the same central character on $G$, they must be isomorphic so long as their local $\gamma$-factors (convolved with irreducible supercuspidal representations of $\text{GL}_n(F)$) align perfectly when used with a fixed nontrivial additive character. By incorporating the machinery for partial Bessel functions developed by Cogdell, Shahidi, and the classification of generic representations into classical types, we surpass the existing bound of $1 \leq n \leq r$ found by Jiang and Soudry. Furthermore, we broaden the framework to encompass the notion of "quasi" generic representations and associate them with a corresponding "quasi" Bessel function, thereby enabling computation of central values of the relevant L-functions via results that match this extended classification.

Pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death, has been observed in patients with COVID-19, yet the specific impact of anti-inflammatory drug interventions on this process remains unclear. Utilizing single-cell transcriptome data from leukocytes in both COVID-19 patients and healthy individuals, we developed a stochastic mathematical model focusing on the NOD-like receptor (NLR) pathway, a primary trigger for pyroptosis. This model effectively reproduces the altered transcriptomic states seen in SARS-Co-19 affected cells. Within our model framework, the induction of pyroptosis, the steady-state levels of various cell subpopulations, and the co-occurrence of specific transcriptomic signatures as reported by SARS-Co-19 data were all successfully replicated. Notably, the model predicts that such interventions can reduce the rate of NLR transcript degradation, potentially leading to increased co-expression of certain markers; however, experimental evidence and known biology indicate these anti-inflammatory drugs actually suppress overall inflammation. A crucial insight from our simulations is that these interventions must accelerate a particular non-transcriptional biological switch to lower global inflammation while simultaneously reducing NLR-based co-expression signatures consistent with clinical SARS-Co-19 findings; the existence of this mechanism is currently unverified experimentally. The proposed molecular identity for this elusive switch and its concentration-dependent concentrations are discussed.

In reinforcement learning, exogenous state variables can introduce unpredictable variance into rewards, thereby decelerating the learning process. We provide a formal definition for these exogenous states and rewards, determining the conditions necessary to separate an exogenous Markov Reward Process (which incorporates only exogenous states and rewards) from the underlying endogenous Markov Decision Process (defined by endogenous rewards). Specifically, we formulate a variance-covariance criterion under which Monte Carlo policy evaluations on the endogenous component are more efficient than those applied to the full problem structure, with these efficiency gains extending broadly to reinforcement learning methodologies. Consequently, we present two distinct algorithms designed to detect these exogenous variables. Experimental results on various MDP tasks validate that these approaches are practically viable, offering substantial accelerations to reinforcement learning performance.

Smart contracts are programs running on blockchains, underpinning various cryptocurrencies, and they share vulnerabilities common to software while facing distinct issues. Although static analysis tools exist specifically for various languages including Tezos, they often produce excessive false positives. Additionally, it is frequently necessary to analyze code in multiple possible interpretations due to features like dynamic library selection or integer bit-vector semantics. This paper presents HELLMHOLTZ, a type-based refinement verifier designed to analyze static properties of Tezos smart contracts. The approach resolves issues by statically eliminating false positives and by determining valid interpretations of bit-vector operations through the careful selection of numeric type instances.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) stand as a prevalent deep learning methodology for learning representations of graphs and their nodes. In this work, we propose aligned differential calculus to derive the foundation of graph convolutions through a matched filtering approach. This mathematical framework permits the rewriting of graph convolutions by our developed graph convolution operator, which is defined on non-linear operators acting on neural networks within the graph semi-spectral framework. By writing graph convolutions in this new form, we observe that the filters in the GCN are determined solely the graph's adjacency matrix, which explains why models relying on them often fail to learn informative and diverse node embeddings. This work presents a novel numerical technique designed to solve time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems, specifically targeting smooth material inhomogeneities subjected to plane waves. While applicable across all frequencies as a time-domain framework, the presentation concentrates on the time-harmonic regime. A key feature of the proposed approach lies in its transformation into an equivalent convolution problem with an effective outgoing wave source, achieved by separating scattered and incident acoustic pressure fields. Consequently, traditional time-harmonic strategies—which often struggle due to non-diagonal compactness in the operator—become unnecessary. Instead, the method formulates a variational request within an $hp$-finite element framework, utilizing a standard $dp$-Green's operator that encapsulates both scattering and homogeneous Dirichlet conditions. Consequently, the numerical scheme demonstrates $O(h^{-2})$ convergence in $L^2$ norms, incurs computational expenses comparable to standard $hp$-FEMs for time-harmonic applications, and crucially allows for local $h$-adaptivity, defined as adaptivity to both frequency and material coefficient gradients. Finally, numerical experiments are provided, illustrating convergence patterns and validating $h$-adaptivity.

This study examines volatile isotope ratios in two distinct groups of iron meteorites—specifically the Chelyabinsk cluster and the Benenitra cluster—discovered recently within the inner solar system. By analyzing these samples alongside earlier findings regarding stony-iron meteorites, we establish evidence that inner solar system planetesimals contained wet icy bodies, likely resulting in a mixed composition of silicate and metallic materials. This evidence contradicts the standard inner-out model of planetary formation, which predicts a dry inner solar system and a dry population of inner planetesimals. Our findings suggest a complex, dynamic history of early planet formation involving widespread collisions between water-rich and rocky bodies, potentially explaining the origins of ocean water on early planetary bodies and potentially accounting for the debated existence of a historic "Mars ocean."

Using the algebraic Bethe-ancestor method, we derive exact expressions for form factors of the integrable XXZ chain that is finite in both spatial and spin dimensions. With regard to those specific types of form factors, we demonstrate that their values can be expressed in terms of weights belonging to the representation of the gl$_N$ quantum group which is the type $[1,1,\cdots,1]$. Furthermore, we argue that the subset of form factors belonging to representations with "at most one" Young boxes is obtainable via the application of the appropriate scalar form-factor to the set of form factors discussed earlier. In effect, this finding enables the calculation of many previously inaccessible form factors for the system at hand.

Speech Translation involves converting spoken audio in one language into written text in another. Traditional cascaded systems, which combine an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with a Machine Translation (MT) system, suffer from compounded errors because the translation relies on the raw output of the speech recognizer. In contrast, direct end-to-end approaches, which aim to establish a link between clean speech and written language, face significant hurdles due to the scarcity of simultaneously available training data sets. This study introduces a novel, direct speech translation framework capable of operating in an unsupervised manner using only two separate unaligned speech-language text corpus. The proposed end-to-end model architecture facilitates direct training by creating a virtual implicit speech distribution, effectively simulating a non-existent real speech input. Experiments utilizing two unaligned public speech-language translation benchmarks demonstrate that this zero-shot method achieves promising initial outcomes.

This work evaluates three methodologies for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, Cartesian irreducible multipoles, and spherical multipoles. We conclude that spherical multipoles are optimal for characterizing electromagnetic radiation scattering, a finding demonstrated using an amorphous silicon sphere. Furthermore, these multipoles facilitate the computation of optical forces acting on metallic, dielectric, or semiconducting particles across a broad spectrum ranging from dipolar to full Mie regimes.

This study introduces two novel families: quantum immanants defined on matrices and their double Young-Capelli bitableaux forms shown in prior work by preceding authors. We identify crucial properties of these structures and establish conversion formulas enabling translation between quantum immanants using the standard Young-Capelli bitableaux. Additionally, we introduce the notion of Schur symmetry for powers and shifts of variables within the symmetric group context, along a new class—symmetric functions—which are now termed "Schur shifted." Finally, we present the relationship connecting these functions with double Young-Capelli bitableaux.

We examine the internal coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, alongside phenomenological frameworks for neutrinos and dark matter, using the minimal scoto-seesaw model. By incorporating the model's dark sector into these frameworks, we demonstrate a clear link between vacuum stability, Higgs boson production rates, dark matter relic density, and neutrino masses. Specifically, we identify how the V-top potential depth in the dark sector influences key parameters: higher potential depth results in deeper minima for both the dark sector potential and the Higgs sector, necessitates stronger couplings between dark matter and scoto-sector fields, reduces fermion-neutrino signals relative to the standard scoto-seesaw approach, yields distinct implications for WIMP dark matter, imposes specific constraints on the dark sector behaving as an almost conformal field theory, and establishes definitive relationships between seesaw mechanisms, vacuum structure, Higgs physics, and dark matter.

We analyze the mixing between $e_g$ and $t_{2g}$ $d$-orbital states within a cubic lattice, subject to the influence of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and interactions with non-$d$ states (such as $p$-orbitals of anions), all treated self-consistently using a tight-binding model. Our findings indicate that, contrary to the common approximation of treating these $d$-orbital manifolds as completely separated, such mixing occurs even when limited to a two-level system—specifically, through SOC-induced coupling of $d$-orbitals to anion $p$-orbitals whose energies lie close to those of the $d$-states. At the example of Bismuth Thallium Oxide (BTO), we demonstrate as a case in point how this phenomenon alters the dependence of exchange splitting on tetragonal lattice distortion when evaluated via density functional theory (DFT). Furthermore, we show that modifying the occupancy of hybridizing $e_g$ states becomes a viable mechanism for magnetically stabilizing a metastable $S=1$ state (a Kittlik state) in this material post-formation.

This investigation examines the behavior of relative quantum cohomology, a notion introduced independently by Tseng-You and Fan-Wu-You across birational transformations. For toric complete intersection simple normal crossing divisors $D_i \subset X$, defined by torus-invariant subvarieties $V_i \subset D_i$, the paper presents sufficient conditions ensuring the stability of this concept. The analysis specifically covers toric blowups at fixed points and toric flips. In each scenario, explicitly matched isomorphisms are established between the corresponding relative quantum cohomology spaces, demonstrating their mutual consistency and compatibility.

Utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs), disease-aware image editing represents a significant breakthrough in the management of pulmonary ailments, particularly pneumonia. Although prior research established the capability of GANs to perform such editing while preserving anatomical correctness and aligning with physician knowledge, these studies were confined to data from a single center and a specific pathogen (*S. pneumoniae*). This limitation suggests a need for broader validation. This work expands the study by incorporating chest radiographs from a second institution featuring radiated images of the virus causing COVID-19. This expanded dataset enables a comparative analysis of the radiated outputs associated with the two different diseases.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for the visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial datasets. Designed to handle "row-column" formats where column pairs represent point coordinates along specific axes and remaining columns define associated values or weights, the tool generates 2D or 3D scatter plots enhanced with color gradients, line structures, and shaded surfaces. By performing dimensionality reduction via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project high-dimensional rows into lower-dimensional spaces, it enables intuitive insights into complex data. Complementing these capabilities, a suite of other functions addresses fundamental needs for dataset management, cleaning, and statistical examination.

This application was developed using Python development with Microsoft Visual Studio, making it accessible at no cost via a downloadable executable for Windows 10/11 64-bit (no separate Python installation required) and an included licensed copy of the SciPy library. An extensive, user-oriented manual accompanies the software, which is further supported by an active online community where developers and researchers can exchange ideas and findings.

Accurate and computationally efficient assessment of Newtonian potentials across diverse two-dimensional regions is vital for the numerical solution of Poisson equations and volume integral equations. For intricate shapes, discretization via unstructured grids makes direct potential calculation using quadrature prohibitively expensive. This study proposes a straightforward yet efficient high-order scheme for determining these potentials by employing Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary forms that are well-suited for the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the traditional cost scales from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$, where $N$ denotes the total elements count. This calculated volume potentials are essential for high-performance boundary element techniques that address full-wave electromagnetic scattering and solves for full-wave and force evaluations in general Newtonian problems, often serving as a key sub-routine in multipole/adaptive multiplication algorithms.
